title: Effective-Interest Amortization
description: Calculate interest expense and amortize bond premiums and discounts.
html:
The two interest calculations

This is one of the most important bond concepts. Do not mix these two calculations.

Cash Interest

Face Value × Stated Rate × Time

Interest Expense

Beginning Carrying Amount × Effective Rate × Time

Discount example

Assume:

Face Value $100,000
Stated Annual Rate 6%
Effective Annual Rate 8%
Beginning Carrying Amount $95,000

For this introductory example, assume annual interest payments.

Step 1 — Calculate cash interest

$100,000 × 6% = $6,000

Step 2 — Calculate interest expense

$95,000 × 8% = $7,600

Step 3 — Calculate discount amortization

$7,600 − $6,000 = $1,600

Step 4 — Update carrying amount

$95,000 + $1,600 = $96,600
Beginning Carrying Amount $95,000
Interest Expense $7,600
Cash Interest ($6,000)
Ending Carrying Amount $96,600

Discount rule

Interest Expense > Cash Interest

The difference amortizes the discount, increasing carrying amount.

Premium example

Now assume:

Face Value $100,000
Stated Annual Rate 10%
Effective Annual Rate 8%
Beginning Carrying Amount $105,000

Cash interest

$100,000 × 10% = $10,000

Interest expense

$105,000 × 8% = $8,400

Premium amortization

$10,000 − $8,400 = $1,600

Ending carrying amount

$105,000 − $1,600 = $103,400

Premium rule

Cash Interest > Interest Expense

The difference amortizes the premium, decreasing carrying amount.

The pattern to memorize

Discount

Expense > Cash

Carrying amount ↑

Premium

Cash > Expense

Carrying amount ↓

quiz.prompt: A bond has a $200,000 face value, a 6% stated annual rate, an 8% effective annual rate, and a beginning carrying amount of $190,000. Assuming annual interest payments, what is the first year's discount amortization?
quiz.explanation: Cash interest = $200,000 × 6% = $12,000. Interest expense = $190,000 × 8% = $15,200. Discount amortization = $15,200 − $12,000 = $3,200.

objectives: Explain effective-interest amortization and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
Evaluate common errors and their financial-statement effects.
